'''Flatbush''' is a neighborhood in the [[New York City]] [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]]. The neighborhood consists of several subsections in central Brooklyn and is generally bounded by [[Prospect Park (Brooklyn)|Prospect Park]] to the north, [[East Flatbush, Brooklyn|East Flatbush]] to the east, [[Midwood, Brooklyn|Midwood]] to the south, and [[Kensington, Brooklyn|Kensington]] and Parkville to the west. The modern neighborhood includes or borders several institutions of note, including [[Brooklyn College]].

The area was home to the [[Canarsee]] people before contact with Europeans; many of the tribe's paths would become important roads through the region. Flatbush was originally chartered as the Dutch Nieuw Nederland colony town of Midwout, also called Vlachte Bos. It was one of the six original European towns on Long Island. The town remained primarily Dutch and rural in character until the latter half of the 19th century, when increasing rail and road connectivity to other parts of New York made it an attractive [[suburb]] to Brooklyn and New York City. The town was consolidated into the [[City of Greater New York]] in 1898 and was further connected to the rest of the city with the development of the [[New York City Subway]] in the early 20th century. Post-World War II, the neighborhood underwent tremendous demographic shifts, becoming home to increasing numbers of immigrants from the Caribbean, Asia, and elsewhere. In the late 20th century and 21st century it has continued to see changes due to [[gentrification]] and new immigrants.

Flatbush is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 14|Brooklyn Community District 14]]. It is patrolled by the 67th and 70th Precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]]. Politically, Flatbush is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 40th and 45th Districts.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf Current City Council Districts for Kings County] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131103455/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf |date=January 31, 2017 }}, [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==History==

===Colonial period===
{{New Netherland}}
In the 16th century, western [[Long Island]] was inhabited by the [[Canarsee]] people, who called it Sewanhacka.<ref name="bpl_dutch frontier">{{cite web|url=https://lefferts.brooklynhistory.org/brooklyns-dutch-frontier/|title=Brooklyn's Dutch Frontier|series=An American Family Grows in Brooklyn|website=Lefferts Family Papers|publisher=[[Brooklyn Historical Society]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> The Canarsee and related [[Lenape]] tribes lived semi-nomadic lives, moving seasonally to follow food sources. Their crisscrossing trails through the area formed some of the early roads for the modern region.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=7–8}} One of their primary settlements was located roughly at the current intersection of [[Flatbush Avenue]] and [[Kings Highway (Brooklyn)|Kings Highway]], named Keskachane or "council fire".{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=9–10}}

[[Henry Hudson]] is reported to have landed on the island in 1609.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=15–16}} Hudson was an Englishman working for the Dutch East India Company, and the Dutch established trading posts and settlements in their new colony of [[New Netherland|Nieuw Nederland]] thereafter, buying up land from the Canarsee (who did not share the Dutch's view of property rights, viewing the sales not as final but essentially leases.){{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=9–10}} One of the Dutch settlements was Midwout (alternatively ''Midwoud'' or ''Medwoud'',) Dutch for "middle wood". Midwout was established inland, in a forested area bounded by hills to the north and flat open spaces to the south,{{sfn|Strong|1842|pp=10–11}} which had been managed by the natives for cultivation and game purposes.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|p=16}} The geography was created by the ancient glacier that once covered the area, leaving behind as it retreated the hills of the [[terminal moraine]] and a large outwash plain beyond.<ref name="nytimes_2018-06-05">{{cite news|last=Broad|first=William|date=June 5, 2018|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/05/science/how-the-ice-age-shaped-new-york.html|title=How the Ice Age Shaped New York|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 20, 2023|page=D1}}</ref> Midwout was settled between 1630 and 1636, and received a patent of township by 1652.{{efn|The exact dates for Flatbush's settlement are unclear. Reverend Thomas M. Strong, in his 1842 history of Flatbush, cites the earliest known land deeds for lands lying in Flatbush and nearby Flatlands as June 6, 1636, but concludes "it is not improbable, however, that considerable settlements were made before any formal grants or Patents of lands were obtained." The original patents for Flatbush's township were lost.{{sfn|Strong|1842|pp=10–13}}<!-- specify other dates -->}} In the following years it would also be known as Vlachte Bos or Flackebos ("wooded plain"), and the various names and spellings of the town were used interchangeably for nearly a century.{{sfn|Gody|1939|p=493}}{{sfn|Vanderbilt|1899|p=32–35}}

A church was built in 1654, replaced by another structure in 1698.{{sfn|Gody|1939|p=493}} The early settlement was enclosed by a palisade wall for protection.{{sfn|Gody|1939|p=493}}{{sfn|Strong|1842|p=16}} By 1658, it was the location of the courts and seat of Justice for the county.{{sfn|Strong|1842|p=14}} There were records of schoolmasters in the town from 1659.{{sfn|Vanderbilt|1899|p=21}} The north end of Midwout was called Steenraap, the main business center the Dorp, and the south end Rustenburgh or resting-place.{{sfn|Vanderbilt|1899|p=34–37}} Among the early colonists in Midwout who would rise to prominence was Leffert Pietersen Van Haughwout. Van Haughwout's family, later known as the Lefferts, would build a homestead in the 1680s in the north of town, now part of [[Prospect Lefferts Gardens]].<ref name="brownstoner_2010-12-07">Spellen, Suzanne. [https://www.brownstoner.com/brooklyn-life/walkabout-the-l-3/ "Walkabout: The Lefferts Family, Flatbush Branch"], ''[[Brownstoner Magazine]]'', December 7, 2010. Accessed February 25, 2024.</ref> Other Dutch families would ultimately lend their names to the streets of the modern city.<ref name="nytimes_2015-05-10"/> In its early years, Midwout came into conflict with its neighboring town of New Amersfoort over its borders, as well as with the local natives; in 1670 the Rockaway Indians challenged the Dutch claims, saying the Canarsee had no authority to sell the land. Midwout's leadership bought the land again to avoid trouble. By the end of the century most of the natives in the region were either dead by war or disease, or dispossessed of their ancestral lands; a few remained in Midwout as farmhands or servants for the Dutch.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=9–10}}

In 1664, the English captured nearby [[New Amsterdam]], and New Netherland was ceded to the English, remaining permanently in their hands after 1674 as New York.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=14}} The towns of Long Island were united as [[Brooklyn|Kings County]] in 1683.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=8}} The borders of Midwout were fixed in 1685 in a new charter granted by [[Thomas Dongan]], the English governor of New York province. The English "Flatbush" gradually supplanted the Dutch names for the town.<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-27">{{cite news|date=August 27, 1928|series=1 of 3|title=Flatbush Avenue, With new Flash of Building Activity, Presents Scene of Dash, Vitality and Progressiveness|work=[[Brooklyn Times-Union|Brooklyn Standard Union]]|page=9|url=https://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%25201928%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%25201928%2520-%25208123.pdf%23xml%3Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.fultonhistory.com%2FdtSearch%2Fdtisapi6.dll%3Fcmd%3Dgetpdfhits%26u%3D724a700f%26DocId%3D1138714%26Index%3DZ%253a%255cDISK%2520P%26HitCount%3D14%26hits%3D8%2B9%2Ba%2Bb%2Bc%2Bd%2Be%2Bf%2B10%2B11%2B12%2B13%2B14%2B16%2B%26SearchForm%3D%252fFulton%255fform%252ehtml%26.pdf&uri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%25201928%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Standard%2520Union%25201928%2520-%25208123.pdf&xml=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fultonhistory.com%2FdtSearch%2Fdtisapi6.dll%3Fcmd%3Dgetpdfhits%26u%3D724a700f%26DocId%3D1138714%26Index%3DZ%253a%255cDISK%2520P%26HitCount%3D14%26hits%3D8%2B9%2Ba%2Bb%2Bc%2Bd%2Be%2Bf%2B10%2B11%2B12%2B13%2B14%2B16%2B%26SearchForm%3D%252fFulton%255fform%252ehtml%26.pdf&openFirstHlPage=false}}</ref> The Dutch character of Flatbush remained despite the English takeover; Dutch landowners continued to exert political control, and Dutch remained the dominant language until the latter part of the 18th century. Marriage outside of Dutch social circles was discouraged, which helped retain Dutch culture and kept the inhabitants "clannish", in the words of one historian.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=14–15}}

Early Dutch settlement of the area had focused on farming, which proved lucrative as nearby [[New York City]] grew. The need for labor spurred the importation of African slaves, making New York one of the largest slaveholding regions in the northern English colonies.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|p=28}} Dutch slavery was less rigid and repressive than that of the [[Southern Colonies]], but as the English assumed control of the region, harsher legal codes came into effect.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=30–32}} The slave population swelled through the 18th century. In 1738, 29% of Flatbush's recorded population of 539 were slaves, jumping to 41% by 1790.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|p=28}}{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=16–17}} The enslaved labor pool was also supplemented by [[indentured servitude|indentured servants]] from the British Isles or Germany.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=18}}

During the [[American Revolution]] (1775–1783), Flatbush demonstrated conflicting loyalties to either the loyalist or patriot causes.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=20–21}} Patriot troops burned houses and farmland early in war to deny the British the resources.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=22–23}} Landowners in Brooklyn were concerned that a full conflict between the Colonies and the British would result in loss of their critical source of slave labor.<ref>''The Ordeal of Kings County'' by Edwin G. Burrows as part of Tiedemann and Fingerhut (editors) ''The Other New York: The American Revolution Beyond New York City'' 2005</ref> Parts of the [[Battle of Long Island]] took place in Flatbush; the patriots checked the British advance north at what is now known as [[Battle Pass (Brooklyn)|Battle Pass]], until they were surprised by a flanking attack. The town of Flatbush was occupied by the British for seven years, with British troops and American prisoners of war billeted in area homes.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=22–23}} Some Flatbush residents maintained their loyalist sympathies: the King's Arms, for example, appeared in the town's inn for a half-century after the conclusion of the conflict.{{sfn|Gody|1939}}<!-- page no. needed -->

For several decades after the Revolution, New York merchants and farmers continued to engage in the slave trade. The Gradual Emancipation Law of 1799 emancipated people of African descent born after July 4, 1799. Men and women escaping enslavement often went to Manhattan, where they could live within the community of free blacks. Slavery was fully abolished in 1827, though many former slaves continued to work as sharecroppers under their former owners.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=27–30}}

===19th century===
[[File:Copy of the Map of the Town of Flatbush in Dr Strongs History, 1842.jpg|thumb|Flatbush Old Town in 1842. The triangular intersection at the edge of the town is roughly at the current-day intersection of Flatbush Avenue and East New York Avenue.{{sfn|Vanderbilt|1899|p=236}}]]
[[File:Robinson's atlas of Kings County, New York LOC 2011594778-5 (Flatbush crop).jpg|thumb|300px|Flatbush and surrounding Kings County in 1890, shortly before it was annexed into Brooklyn to the north. The irregular Flatbush streets have been replaced with a street grid; its borders have been encroached upon by [[Green-Wood Cemetery]] and Prospect Park.]]
Into the 19th century, Flatbush remained a slow-growing farming community.<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-27"/> The opening of the [[Erie Canal]] shifted cultivation away from grains and towards market produce, with Kings County being the second-largest provider of produce in the country until the end of the century after Queens County.<ref name="bpl_farming">{{cite web|url=https://lefferts.brooklynhistory.org/farming-brooklyn/|title=Farming Brooklyn|series=An American Family Grows in Brooklyn|website=Lefferts Family Papers|publisher=[[Brooklyn Historical Society]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> It remained isolated from the growing Brooklyn by open country. [[Prospect Park (Brooklyn)|Prospect Park]] was developed from land partially in Flatbush, though it was wholly claimed by Brooklyn.<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-27"/> The rural character of the town, however, would not last. In the second quarter of the century, a street grid was laid out, and the main north–south road was established as Flatbush Avenue.<ref name="lpc_1973-10-16"/> A stream of Irish and some German immigrants arrived in the area, comprising the majority of the rural labor force by 1860.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=32–33}} Though Flatbush and Kings County did not support [[Abraham Lincoln]]'s presidency in 1860, after the [[American Civil War]] broke out, Flatbush residents raised funds and soldiers for the war effort. Blacks fleeing the violence of the [[New York City draft riots]] found refuge in Flatbush and nearby [[Weeksville, Brooklyn|Weeksville]].{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=33–35}}

Flatbush built a [[Flatbush Town Hall|Town Hall]] in 1875, a few years after Flatbush and the other towns of Kings County avoided annexation by Brooklyn.<ref name="lpc_1973-10-16">{{cite web|date=October 16, 1973|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0770.pdf|title=Flatbush Town Hall, 35 Snyder Avenue|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> The [[Brooklyn, Flatbush and Coney Island Railway]], established 1878, connected Flatbush to the pleasure spots at [[Coney Island]] and the Atlantic Coast to the south, and downtown Brooklyn and Manhattan to the north.<ref name="bpl_developing"/> The railways and the opening of bridges connecting Brooklyn to Manhattan began transforming Flatbush into a [[suburb]].<ref name="lpc_1978-07-11">{{cite web|date=July 11, 1978|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0989.pdf|title=Albemarle-Kenmore Terraces Historic District |publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> Towards the end of the century, the land was worth more if used for real estate than farming, and large landowners began selling off plots.<ref name="bpl_developing"/>{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=40}} John Lefferts divided his family's Flatbush homestead into 516 parcels, restricted by covenant to only be developed into single-family housing.<ref name="bpl_developing">{{cite web|url=https://lefferts.brooklynhistory.org/developing-brooklyn/|title=Developing Brooklyn|series=An American Family Grows in Brooklyn|website=Lefferts Family Papers|publisher=[[Brooklyn Historical Society]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> These formed Lefferts Manor, containing possibly the neighborhood's earliest [[row house]]s.<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/> Another early development was Vanderveer Park, formed from 65 acres of the Vanderveer family's holdings.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=40}} Like Lefferts Manor, Vanderveer Park traded on the Dutch history of the region to attract buyers. The developers of the new housing pitched Flatbush as a country oasis offering respite from the "cliff-dwelling" vertical living of Manhattan.<ref name="nytimes_2008-03-16">{{cite news|last=Lerner|first=Evan|date=March 16, 2008|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/03/16/nyregion/thecity/16vict.html|title=Peaked Roofs, Crossed Fingers|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref>{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=40}} Much of the development focused on the areas immediately south and east of Prospect Park, with the farther-flung areas remaining mostly rural and dotted with wood-framed houses.<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17">{{cite web|last=Caratzas|first=Michael|date=November 17, 2020|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2647.pdf|title=East 25th Street Historic District|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref>

Amid the construction of houses and the infrastructure to support them, Flatbush's population tripled in the decades before 1900.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=43}} In the face of increasing urbanization, some community leaders wished for Flatbush and the outlying Kings County towns to retain their rural character.{{sfn|McGee|2005|p=31}}{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=39}} Resident and amateur historian Gertrude Lefferts Vanderbilt, writing in 1881, correctly predicted a coming merger with Brooklyn, and lamented that the Dutch character of the town was gone.<ref name="bpl_chronicling">{{cite web|url=https://lefferts.brooklynhistory.org/chronicling-brooklyn/|title=Chronicling Brooklyn|series=An American Family Grows in Brooklyn|website=Lefferts Family Papers|publisher=[[Brooklyn Historical Society]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> The only remaining signs of its presence to her were "the reminiscences and traditions, while the old family names mark the localities still, as the projecting peaks mark the submerged rock."{{sfn|Vanderbilt|1899|p=9}}

In 1894, Flatbush was successfully annexed into Brooklyn. A reception hosting Brooklyn mayor [[Charles A. Schieren]] was held at the Midwood Club House, where Schieren called the former town "the prettiest and most fascinating suburban village of Kings County."<ref name="brooklyneagle_1894-05-20">{{cite news|date=May 20, 1894|title=Music, Speeches, Good Cheer, All Combined, at the Flatbush Annexation Celebration|work=[[The Brooklyn Daily Eagle]]|page=24}}</ref> Brooklyn itself was merged into New York City in 1898, a move opposed by many in Brooklyn and passed by just 277 votes.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=8–9}}

===20th century===
In the early 20th century, Flatbush changed even more rapidly as further transit improvements spurred additional development.<ref name="bpl_chronicling"/><ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/> The course of the Brooklyn, Flatbush & Coney Island Railroad (now called the Brooklyn & Brighton Beach Railroad) was electrified in 1901 and run over the [[Brooklyn Bridge]], connecting Flatbush more directly with lower Manhattan. This was followed by further improvements to the line in the subsequent years, including the addition of more tracks and removal of at-grade crossings. The railways lived alongside five trolley lines that ran to Williamsburg in north Brooklyn and the Lower East Side in Manhattan.<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/> Development of the north end of Flatbush was helped along with the construction of [[Ebbets Field]], home of the [[Brooklyn Dodgers]] baseball team.{{sfn|McGee|2005|p=76}}

Construction across Brooklyn slowed as Europe and then America became embroiled in [[World War I]]; the cost of construction spiked, and the city emerged from the war years having gone from a surplus of housing a decade earlier to a dire shortage.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=300–301}} The response from the government was a slew of housing and tenant bills, with one allowing the city to exempt new residential construction from property taxes until 1932. The ordinance spurred a housing boom across the borough, with significant development in the much cheaper land of southern Brooklyn and Flatbush, which was increasingly connected to the rest of the city via new infrastructure projects.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=302–303}} Extant homes—including the neighborhood's earliest suburban development—were converted to multifamily dwellings or demolished for new homes or apartments,<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/><ref name="nytimes_2008-03-16"/> which came in an array of architectural styles.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=304–307}} Alongside the residential construction came commercial developments, from movie palaces like the [[Loew's Kings Theatre]] to department stores like [[Sears Roebuck & Company Department Store (Brooklyn)|Sears Roebuck & Company]]. An entertainment and commercial district developed in the vicinity of Church and Flatbush Avenues,<ref name="lpc_2012-05-15">{{cite web|author=Postal, Matthew|date=May 15, 2012|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2469.pdf|title=Sears Roebuck & Company Department Store|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=August 2, 2020|archive-date=September 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210919022200/http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2469.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> with another developing at the intersection of Flatbush, Avenue H, and Nostrand Avenue, known as the Junction.<ref name="nytimes_2007-12-02"/>

As six-story [[Art Deco]] and [[Colonial Revival architecture|Colonial Revival]] elevator apartment houses alongside stylistically analogous walk-ups were developed on Ocean Avenue and throughout its periphery,<ref>{{cite book | last=Allbray | first=N.C. | title=Flatbush: The Heart of Brooklyn | publisher=Arcadia Pub. | series=Making of America series | year=2004 | isbn=978-0-7385-2453-5 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1L2mNAil4BsC | access-date=June 21, 2020 | page=124}}</ref> Flatbush nurtured a socioeconomically diverse population of [[Irish Americans]], [[Italian Americans]] and [[American Jews]]; according to anthropologist Ansley Hamid, occupants ranged from "merchants [and] professionals" to "skilled [and] manual laborers."{{sfn|Hamid|2002|p=128}} By 1930, one-third of Flatbush's residents were Jewish.<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/> The new residents ultimately displaced the remaining Anglo-Dutch, who decamped to farther-off suburbs in Long Island or New Jersey.{{sfn|Campanella|2019|pp=9}}

By the [[Great Depression]], Flatbush had a population of 400,000, and boasted fifteen theaters, rail and trolly lines, dozens of schools, fifty-four churches, and five newspapers.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=49–50}} New York greatly benefited from [[New Deal]] policies and funds,<ref name="golway_2009-04-15">{{cite web|last=Golway|first=Terry|date=April 15, 2009|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/19/nyregion/long-island/19Rwpa.html|title=W.P.A. Projects Left Their Stamp on the Region|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=August 22, 2023|archive-date=August 22, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230822144101/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/19/nyregion/long-island/19Rwpa.html|url-status=live}}</ref> which helped build [[Brooklyn College]] in 1935.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=50}} During [[World War II]] the "soldier from Flatbush" became a symbol of the All-American soldier.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=53}}

After the war, Flatbush saw demographic shifts along with the rest of the city. Owners and renters from the interwar years aged, and their children moved out of the neighborhood; from 1950 to 1960 children under six in Flatbush dropped 14 percent, while the number of seniors over 65 rose 42 percent.<ref name="nytimes_1968-02-14"/> The Dodgers left Brooklyn, and Ebbets Field was torn down.<ref name="nytimes_2013-04-04">{{cite news|last=Anderson|first=Dave|date=April 3, 2013|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/04/sports/baseball/ebbets-field-is-gone-but-memories-of-brooklyn-dodgers-endure.html|title=Echoes of Ebbets Field as It Turns 100|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=March 26, 2024|page=B13}}</ref> In the 1960s, poorer African Americans and Puerto Ricans began moving into the corridor along [[Nostrand Avenue]], where the subway offered access to job opportunities, while middle-class African Americans bought up row houses to the west. [[Blockbusting]] encouraged white residents to sell and leave the neighborhood, and properties fell into disrepair while crime increased.<ref name="nytimes_1968-02-14">{{cite news|last=|first=|date=February 14, 1968|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1968/02/14/89320587.html?zoom=14.92|title=After Era of Stability, Flatbush Yields to Change|work=[[The New York Times]]|pages=49, 54}}</ref>{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=58–59}} The population of the neighborhood shifted from 89% white in 1970 to 30% white in a decade. The white and Jewish residents were replaced by Hispanic, Asian, and black ones, and the commercial properties shifted to reflect the change.<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/> Afro-Caribbean immigrants joined African Americans in moving from traditional neighborhoods like Harlem to Flatbush, particularly Haitians fleeing the dictatorial rule of [[François Duvalier|François]] and [[Jean-Claude Duvalier]].<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/> One resident who moved to the area in 1971 recalled that his building gradually shed staff and maintenance was neglected as the decade wore on, amid a wider drop in city services following the [[1975 New York City fiscal crisis|city's financial crisis]].{{sfn|Hamid|2002|pp=127–129}}

Parts of the neighborhood in the west and to the south of Prospect Park continued to attract a sizable number of wealthier homeowners, and doctors still resided and practiced on a stretch of Parkside Avenue immediately adjacent to Prospect Park. By the mid-1980s, however, the neighborhood had numerous abandoned or semi-abandoned buildings, many of which had fallen into a state of disrepair. The eastern parts of Flatbush were particularly affected.<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/>{{sfn|Hamid|2002|pp=127–129}} Crime worsened significantly during the 1970s and 80s,<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/> alongside a rise in drugs.<ref>{{cite web | last=Rohde | first=David | title=Where Has Your Neighborhood Drug Dealer Gone? | website=[[The New York Times]] | date=August 17, 1997 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/08/17/nyregion/where-has-your-neighborhood-drug-dealer-gone.html | access-date=February 3, 2017|at=Section 13, page 1}}</ref><!-- this talks about the police presence in Flatbush, but less specifically about the drugs and scale of the problem in the neighborhood. Should find a better ref. --> A number of stores on Flatbush and Church Avenues fell victim to looting during the [[New York City blackout of 1977|1977 blackout]].<ref>{{cite web | author=Moritz|first=Owen|title=Looters prey on the city during the blackout of 1977 | website=[[New York Daily News]] | date=July 12, 2015 | url=http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/nyc-crime/looters-prey-city-blackout-1977-article-1.2284260 | access-date=February 3, 2017}}</ref>
[[File:1024x768-dsc04118.jpg|thumb|left|Church and Flatbush, 2013]]
Tenants rights organizations and neighborhood associations formed to fight back against the neighborhood's decay. The Flatbush Development Corporation, one of a number of [[community development corporation]]s that formed in poorer areas of the country starting in the late 1960s, sought to revitalize the community. The FDC investigated bad landlords and agitated for loans to developers willing to refurbish old buildings.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=60}} Other groups worked to protect threatened buildings and neighborhoods as [[historic landmark]]s.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=62–63}} In the 1980s, families and young couples priced out of areas like [[Park Slope]] and looking for cheaper real estate moved into the homes in the historic areas.<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/> Residents started buying their houses and forming block associations;<ref name="lpc_2020-11-17"/><ref name="newyorkmag_1987-05-04"/><!-- that ref is for a single one, use the western ones as well, mention preservation efforts, CORTELYOU  --> the high percentage of buyers who were middle-class black residents made it atypical from other gentrification waves on the time in the city that displaced the current residents.<ref name="nytimes_1989-04-16">{{cite news|last=Peterson|first=Iver|date=April 16, 1989|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/16/realestate/co-op-waves-washing-over-flatbush.html|title=Co-op Waves Washing Over Flatbush|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=January 26, 2024|at=Section 10, p. 1}}</ref> Owners in the [[Prospect Park South]] neighborhood hired private security to patrol the neighborhood.<ref name="newyorkmag_1987-05-04">{{cite magazine|last=Tyre|first=Peg|date=May 4, 1987|title=Flatbush; Touches of the Dutch and Turn-of-the-Century Grandeur|magazine=[[New York Magazine]]|volume=20|issue=18|pages=64–66}}</ref> Residents lobbied commercial business to return to the area.<ref name="nytimes_2002-07-07">{{cite news|last=Kugel|first= Seth|date=July 7, 2002|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/07/07/nyregion/neighborhood-report-flatbush-victorian-area-is-tired-of-being-discounted.html|title=Neighborhood Report: Flatbush; Victorian Area Is Tired of Being Discounted|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=February 25, 2024}}</ref> Local merchants, the city, and the Flatbush Development Corporation worked to revitalize the neighborhood's commercial core. The Flatbush Avenue Business Improvement District was founded in 1990, and by 1996 included 195 merchants on the stretch of road between Parkside Avenue and Cortelyou Road.<ref name="nytimes_1996-11-03">{{cite news|last=Kershaw|first=Sarah|date=November 3, 1996|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/11/03/nyregion/flatbush-ave-renaissance-brings-hope-for-kings.html|title=Flatbush Ave. Renaissance Brings Hope For Kings|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2023|at=Section 13, p. 10}}</ref>

===21st century===
[[File:Environmentalist banner at Beverly Road Station.jpg|thumb|View of residential house with [[Extinction Rebellion]] banner at [[Beverly Road station|Beverly Road Station]] in Flatbush]]
In the 2000s, Flatbush began to shed its poor reputation, and residents came to the area for its cheaper prices, attractive housing stock, and retail.<ref name="nytimes_2007-12-02"/> The Junction was redeveloped with the addition of [[Target Corporation]]'s largest-ever store.<ref name="nytimes_2008-09-02">{{cite news|last=Siwolop|first=Sana|date=September 2, 2008|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/03/realestate/commercial/03junction.html|title=Big Stores in Odd Shapes Arriving in Brooklyn|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 21, 2023}}</ref> The demographics of the neighborhood continued to shift; new Jewish residents from Syria arrived alongside Pakistanis, Bangladeshis, Russians, and Chinese.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|pp=64–68}} The Muslim community was hit hard in the aftermath of the [[September 11 attacks|September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks]]; an estimated 20,000 residents left voluntarily or otherwise after immigration crackdowns.{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=68}} Recognizing the changed makeup of the eastern part of the neighborhood, the city designated two areas "[[Little Caribbean, Brooklyn|Little Caribbean]]" and "<span class="anchor" id="Little Haiti">[[Little Haiti, Brooklyn|Little Haiti]]</span>" in 2017 and 2018, respectively.<ref name="nytimes_2018-04-17">{{cite news|last=Mays|first=Jeffrey|date=April 17, 2018|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/04/17/nyregion/brooklyn-little-haiti.html|title=In Brooklyn, Push for a Special Haitian District Hits Resistance|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 21, 2023|at=Section A, p. 17}}</ref><ref name="nytimes_2018-07-05">{{cite news|last=Mays|first=Jeffrey|date=July 5, 2018|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/05/nyregion/little-haiti-flatbush-brooklyn-street.html|title=What's in a Name? Plenty, When It's a Street in Brooklyn's 'Little Haiti'|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 21, 2023|at=Section A, p. 17}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://columbianewsservice.com/2023/10/27/little-haiti-feels-like-home-for-immigrants-in-brooklyns-flatbush-neighborhood/|date=27 October 2023|publisher=Columbia News Service|title=‘Little Haiti’ Feels Like Home for Immigrants in Brooklyn’s Flatbush Neighborhood}}</ref> Little Haiti is bounded by Church and Brooklyn Avenues to the west, East 16th Street to the north, Avenue H and Parkside Avenue to the south, and East 16th Street<ref>{{cite web|url=https://legistar.council.nyc.gov/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=3538103&GUID=D86C2A6F-CE2A-4C41-A14E-E46155A8BA21&Options=&Search=#:~:text=The%20New%20York%20City%20Council%20%2D%20File%20%23:%20Res%200423%2D2018&text=Name:,%2C%20as%20%E2%80%9CLittle%20Haiti%E2%80%9D.&text=Enactment%20date:,%2C%20as%20%22Little%20Haiti%22.&text=Ver.&text=423-,Resolution%20ceremonially%20designating%20Flatbush%20Brooklyn%2C%20within%20the%20boundaries%20of%20East,%2C%20as%20%E2%80%9CLittle%20Haiti%E2%80%9D.&text=Resolved%2C%20That%20the%20Council%20of,%2C%20as%20%E2%80%9CLittle%20Haiti.%E2%80%9D|website=New York City Council|title=Res 0423-2018 Version: *}}</ref> to the east.

The ''Times'' featured the neighborhood in 2016 as one of four in the city where real estate was expected to take off, as buyers looked for more affordable options.<ref name="hot">{{cite news|last=Higgins|first=Michelle|date=February 26, 2016|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/28/realestate/new-yorks-next-hot-neighborhoods.html|title=New York's Next Hot Neighborhoods|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929073223/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/28/realestate/new-yorks-next-hot-neighborhoods.html |archive-date=September 29, 2017|url-status=live|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 22, 2023|page=RE1}}</ref> Flatbush was disparately impacted by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] compared to higher-income parts of the city.<ref name="bklyner_2021-08-13">[https://bklyner.com/brooklyn-census-2020/ "What Does the New Census Data Tell Us About Brooklyn?"], [[Bklyner]], August 13, 2021. Accessed February 25, 2024.</ref> As housing prices have increased,<ref name="gothamist_2022-09-02">Ibrahim, Shamira. [https://gothamist.com/news/flatbush-residents-cautiously-optimistic-about-west-indian-day-parades-return-after-two-year-hiatus "Flatbush residents cautiously optimistic about West Indian Day parade’s return after two-year hiatus"], ''[[Gothamist]]'', September 2, 2022. Accessed February 25, 2024.</ref> the neighborhood's predominantly black population has begun to shrink.<ref name="cuny_2023-01-20">{{cite web|last1=Mollenkopf|first1=John|last2=Blair|first2=Zulema|last3=Hum|first3=Tarry|last4=Lipsitz|first4=Keena|last5=Rivera-Burgos|first5=Viviana|last6=Romalewski|first6=Steven|last7=Bauer|first7=Valerie|date=January 20, 2023|url=https://nycoi2023.commons.gc.cuny.edu/nyc-communities-of-interest-report-2023/|title=How Communities of Interest Are Evolving in New York City Today|website=[[City University of New York]]|access-date=December 22, 2023}}</ref>

The neighborhood continues to face issues as a lower-income neighborhood compared to the city, with a 2016 [[WNYC]] reporting finding the neighborhood was disproportionately the target of [[Vision Zero]] traffic safety enforcement compared to whiter neighborhoods like [[Williamsburg, Brooklyn|Williamsburg]] and [[Greenpoint, Brooklyn|Greenpoint]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Santore|first=John|date=August 26, 2016|url=https://patch.com/new-york/ditmaspark/flatbush-activists-want-know-where-nypd-stopping-brooklyn-drivers |title=Flatbush Activists Want to Know Where the NYPD is Stopping Brooklyn Drivers |website=[[Patch Media|Patch]] |access-date=February 6, 2018 |archive-date=February 7, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207005130/https://patch.com/new-york/ditmaspark/flatbush-activists-want-know-where-nypd-stopping-brooklyn-drivers |url-status=live }}</ref> A 2023 ''[[Gothamist]]'' analysis of 311 data revealed the neighborhood was one of the largest problem areas in the city for illegal waste dumping.<ref name="gothamist_2023-01-31">{{cite web|last=Chang|first=Sophia|date=January 31, 2023|url=https://gothamist.com/news/illegal-dumping-trashes-nycs-lower-income-areas|title=Illegal dumping trashes NYC's lower-income areas|website=[[Gothamist]]|access-date=January 2, 2024}}</ref>

Little remains of the original Flatbush village and its surroundings. The 18th-century [[Lefferts Historic House|Lefferts family house]], which resided in Flatbush, was moved in 1918 from its original location to Prospect Park along Flatbush Avenue.<ref name="nytimes_2015-05-10"/> Near the Lefferts house is a former toll booth from the 19th century that once sat along the Flatbush Turnpike leading to Brooklyn.<ref name="brownstoner_2018-04-23">{{cite web|last=De Vries|first=Susan|date=April 23, 2018|url=https://www.brownstoner.com/architecture/prospect-park-flatbush-avenue-tollbooth-brooklyn-history/|title=The Quirky Wooden Relic of Brooklyn's Transit Past in Prospect Park|website=[[Brownstoner Magazine]]|access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> Other historic houses nearby include the [[Wyckoff-Bennett Homestead]], built 1766,<ref name="nytimes_2015-05-10">{{cite news|last=Pollak|first=Michael|date=May 8, 2015|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/10/nyregion/surviving-remnants-of-the-village-of-flatbush.html|title=FYI: Surviving Remnants of the Village of Flatbush|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 20, 2023|page=MB3}}</ref> and the [[Wyckoff House]], built on Twiller's Flats.<ref name="lpc_1965-10-14">{{cite web|date=October 14, 1965|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0001.pdf|title=Pieter Claesen Wyckoff House, Clarendon Road and Ralph Avenue|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=January 11, 2023}}</ref> A marker in Prospect Park marks the site of Battle Pass. The [[Flatbush Reformed Dutch Church Complex|Flatbush Reformed Dutch Church]] remains at the historic center of Flatbush at Church and Flatbush Avenues.<ref name="nytimes_2015-05-10"/>

==Geographic boundaries==
<!-- bit about historical flatbush as a large area, and the town being centered on Flatbush/Church -->When Flatbush merged with Brooklyn, the old town became coterminous with the 29th [[Wards of New York City|ward]].<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-28">{{cite news|date=August 28, 1928|series=2 of 3|title=Flatbush Avenue, With Acres of New Apartment Buildings, is Historic Town With Old Traditions Being Retained|work=[[Brooklyn Times-Union|Brooklyn Standard Union]]|page=3}}</ref> There are no official boundaries for the modern neighborhood,{{efn|New York City deliberately does not have official neighborhood borders, with a spokesperson for the city's planning department saying in 2023 that the city leaves the delineation "up to New Yorkers themselves."<ref name="nytimes_2023-10-29">{{cite web|last=Buchanan|first=Larry|date=October 29, 2023|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/10/29/upshot/new-york-neighborhood-guide.html|title=An Extremely Detailed Guide to an Extremely Detailed Map of New York City Neighborhoods|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2023}}</ref>}} which is smaller than the old boundaries of the town, and have long been disputed.<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-27"/><ref name="nytimes_2007-12-02"/> In 1928, the ''[[Brooklyn Times-Union|Brooklyn Standard Union]]'' gave an expansive definition of Flatbush as running from [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]] in the west to Schenectady Avenue in the east, and from Prospect Park in the north as far south as [[Sheepshead Bay]].<ref name="standardunion_1928-08-27"/> By the 1960s, the northern region of the neighborhood was now considered part of [[Crown Heights, Brooklyn|Crown Heights]] instead.<ref name="nytimes_1968-02-14"/> 1980s ''New York Times'' articles, following the definition of the Flatbush Development Corporation, outlined the narrow boundaries as Parkside Avenue to the north, Bedford Avenue to the east, Avenue H to the south, and [[Coney Island Avenue]] to the west. However they also noted that some residents still considered Midwood part of Flatbush, and the historic definitions had it stretch from Ocean Parkway to New York Avenue.<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30">{{cite news|last=Motyka|first=Joan|date=January 30, 1983|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1983/01/30/200373.html?zoom=15.73|title=If You're Thinking Of Living In: Flatbush|work=[[The New York Times]]|page=R9}}</ref><ref name="nytimes_1989_06_04">{{cite news|last=Lyons|first=Richard|date=June 4, 1989|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/04/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-flatbush.html|title=If You're Thinking Of Living In: Flatbush|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2023|at=Section 10, p. 11}}</ref> By the 2000s, the ''Times'' had shifted the boundaries eastward, with New York Avenue the eastern border and Ocean Avenue the western one;<ref name="nytimes_2007-12-02"/><ref name="nytimes_2015-05-06">{{cite web|last=Konrad|first=Walencia|date=May 6, 2015|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/10/realestate/flatbush-brooklyn-a-fit-for-many-tastes-and-budgets.html|title=Flatbush, Brooklyn, a Fit for Many Tastes and Budgets|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 18, 2023}}</ref> the paper also noted that the area is one with fuzzier boundaries, compared to neighborhoods with sharp, widely-agreed-upon delineations.<ref name="nytimes_2023-10-29"/> The borders roughly coincide with [[Brooklyn Community Board 14|Brooklyn Community District 14]], which also includes portions of Midwood and Kensington.<ref name="Brooklyn Community Board 14">{{cite web |title=District Map |url=https://cb14brooklyn.com/about/district-map/ |access-date=December 19, 2023 |website=Brooklyn Community Board 14|date=February 4, 2023 }}</ref>

Over time, neighborhoods once considered part of Flatbush have gained their own distinct identities.<ref name="nytimes_2007-12-02">{{cite news|last=Bleyer|first=Jennifer|date=December 2, 2007|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/02/realestate/02livi.html|title=Note to City Dwellers: Steals Available Here|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 21, 2023}}</ref> This includes [[Prospect Lefferts Gardens]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Besonen |first=Julie |date=February 1, 2017 |title=Prospect-Lefferts Gardens, Brooklyn: Diverse, Historic and Convenient |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/02/01/realestate/prospect-lefferts-gardens-brooklyn-diverse-historic-and-convenient.html |access-date=December 24, 2023 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and also the various planned communities of [[Victorian Flatbush]]: [[Prospect Park South]],<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/> the [[Beverley Squares]] (Beverley Square East and Beverley Square West),{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=5}} [[Ditmas Park, Brooklyn|Ditmas Park]],<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/> Fiske Terrace,<ref name="nytimes_2011-07-29">{{cite news|last=Berger|first=Joseph|date=July 29, 2011|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/30/nyregion/victorian-flatbush-area-protests-very-modern-pole.html|title=In an Early 1900s Neighborhood, a Glimpse of '2001'|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 19, 2023|page=A19}}</ref>, and [[Albemarle-Kenmore Terraces Historic District|Albemarle-Kenmore Terrace]].<ref name="nytimes_1983-01-30"/>{{sfn|Back|Morrone|2008|p=5}} Bordering Flatbush on the north is Crown Heights, to the east is [[East Flatbush, Brooklyn|East Flatbush]], to the west is Kensington and Parkville, and to the south is Midwood.

==Demographics==

Covering an area of {{convert|1038.56|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|101.9|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610175331/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. == Health ==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s are more common in Flatbush and Midwood than in other places citywide, though births to teenage mothers are less common. In Flatbush and Midwood, there were 99 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 17.1 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Flatbush and Midwood has a relatively high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]], or who receive healthcare through [[Medicaid]].<ref name=":14">[http://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/dsrip/pps_applications/docs/maimonides_medical_center/3.8_maimonides_cna.pdf New York City Health Provider Partnership Brooklyn Community Needs Assessment: Final Report] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723064434/https://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/dsrip/pps_applications/docs/maimonides_medical_center/3.8_maimonides_cna.pdf |date=July 23, 2018 }}, [[New York Academy of Medicine]] (October 3, 2014).</ref> In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 16%, which is higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Flatbush and Midwood is {{convert|0.0077|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, lower than the citywide and boroughwide averages.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Ten percent of Flatbush and Midwood residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is slightly lower than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Flatbush and Midwood, 28% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 13% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 31% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 21% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is lower than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 77% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", slightly less than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Flatbush and Midwood, there are 21 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

Major hospitals in close proximity to Flatbush include [[Kings County Hospital]] and [[SUNY Downstate Medical Center]].<ref name=":14"/> The facilities are located in neighboring [[East Flatbush]] just east of New York Avenue.

==Government and education==
Flatbush is covered by [[ZIP Code]]s 11203, 11210, 11225, and 11226.<ref>{{cite web | title=NYC Neighborhood ZIP Code Definitions | website=New York State Department of Health | date=November 7, 2014 | url=https://www.health.ny.gov/statistics/cancer/registry/appendix/neighborhoods.htm | access-date=March 5, 2019 | archive-date=March 27, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190327233549/https://www.health.ny.gov/statistics/cancer/registry/appendix/neighborhoods.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Flatbush and Midwood generally has a similar ratio of college-educated residents to the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. Though 43% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 18% have less than a high school education and 39% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 40% of Brooklynites and 38% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Flatbush and Midwood students excelling in math rose from 43 percent in 2000 to 68 percent in 2011, though reading achievement remained steady at 48% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/BK_14_11.pdf|title=Flatbush / Midwood – BK 14|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Flatbush and Midwood's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is about equal to the rest of New York City. In Flatbush and Midwood, 18% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], compared to the citywide average of 20% of students.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 75% of high school students in Flatbush and Midwood graduate on time, equal to the citywide average of 75% of students.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

Flatbush is home to a number of elementary and intermediate schools, as well as the [[Erasmus Hall High School]] campus.  Founded in 1786, it has a long list of famous alumni.  Its building has been expanded numerous times, and is notable for its relatively unique architecture.  Since 1994, the building has been divided internally into five smaller high schools, each concentrating on a different academic area.

Brooklyn College (one of the four-year colleges in the [[City University of New York]] system) occupies a {{convert|35|acre|adj=on}} campus shared between the neighborhoods of Flatbush and [[Midwood, Brooklyn|Midwood]].<ref>[http://www.brooklyn.cuny.edu/web/about/campus/visit.php Maps and Directions] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026171951/http://www.brooklyn.cuny.edu/web/about/campus/visit.php |date=October 26, 2016 }}, [[Brooklyn College]]. Accessed October 25, 2016. "Brooklyn College is located on a 35-acre campus in the Midwood / Flatbush neighborhoods. The college is easily accessible by car and public transportation."</ref>

=== Libraries ===
The [[Brooklyn Public Library]] (BPL) has three branches in Flatbush. The Flatbush branch is located at 22 Linden Boulevard east of Flatbush Avenue. It was built in 1905 as a [[List of Carnegie libraries in New York City|Carnegie library branch]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/flatbush|title=Flatbush Library|date=August 22, 2011|website=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> The Clarendon branch is located at 2035 Nostrand Avenue south of Farragut Road. It was founded as a deposit station with a small circulating collection in 1913. The branch moved into its current building in 1954, and it was renovated in 1990.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/clarendon|title=Clarendon Library|date=August 19, 2011|website=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> The Crown Heights branch, located on the border with Crown Heights, is located at 560 New York Avenue near Maple Street.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/crown-heights|title=Crown Heights Library|date=August 19, 2011|website=Brooklyn Public Library|access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>
